Réaction inflammatoire locale, souvent douloureuse, affectant un tissu ou un organe exposé à un agent irritant (chimique, physique ou infectieux).

examples.text: L’application de ce médicament sur la peau y détermine une irritation très vive. Ses nerfs sont dans une grande irritation.

glosses: Action exercée par un stimulus irritant sur un tissu vivant, notamment les nerfs ou les muqueuses.
Effet local, non corrosif, provoqué par un agent chimique sur un tissu vivant, se traduisant par une inflammation réversible.
État émotionnel de tension ou d’agacement, mêlé d’impatience, pouvant évoluer vers la colère.

examples.text: Son irritation fut très vive. J’ai tâché d’adoucir son irritation. Calmer l’irritation des esprits.
Et, peu à peu, de la douceur primordiale, un peu timide et avide de tendresse de son caractère, montaient une sourde irritation, une rancœur et une révolte.

glosses: Agitation ou exaspération collective dans un contexte social ou politique.

examples.text: […]; l'assassinat de la duchesse de Praslin, par son mari, pair de France, accrurent l'irritation publique.

glosses: The act of irritating or annoying.

examples.text: What irritation causes you to be so moody?

glosses: The state of being irritated.

examples.text: It has already been established that the crew was competent and qualified for operation of AS66. With the exception of some overtones of irritation about the manner in which another aircraft, N799Y, affected the flight's progress into the Juneau area, the recorded cockpit conversation, in general, reflects a relaxed but businesslike atmosphere.

Last spring, the periodical cicadas emerged across eastern North America. Their vast numbers and short above-ground life spans inspired awe and irritation in humans—and made for good meals for birds and small mammals.

glosses: To forcefully move or push (someone or something) in a certain direction.

examples.text: Reg[an]. VVherefore to Douer ſir? / Gloſt[er, i.e., Gloucester]. Becauſe I vvould not ſee thy cruell nayles / Pluck out his poore old eyes, nor thy fierce ſiſter / In his aurynted fleſh raſh boriſh phangs, […]

glosses: To break (something) forcefully; to smash.

examples.text:
Fair lordes sayd syre Launcelot leue your noyse and your rassyng and I shalle sette open this dore and thenne may ye doo with me what it lyketh yow.
"Fair lords, said Sir Launcelot, leave your noise and your rashing, and I shall set open this door, and then may ye do with me what it liketh you."

glosses: To emit or issue (something) hastily.
Usually followed by up: to prepare (something) with haste; to cobble together, to improvise.

examples.text: Retur[n]e to the places of Peter, the one in his firſt epiſtle, the other in the latter: and ſo be you contented with this preſent anſvver raſhed up in haſte.

glosses: To move forcefully, hastily, or suddenly; to dash, to rush.
To fall heavily; to dash down.

examples.text: […] the rain rashed down - the road was battered, As with the force of billows shattered; […]
... rain rashed down. The sound was as of a deluge, and all the parched lips of earth seemed to be drinking in the delicious moisture.
Thunder rumbled and a light rain rashed down as Bella shoveled the pile of loose dirt back into the ground.

glosses: To collide or hit.
Acting too quickly without considering the consequences and risks; not careful; hasty.

examples.text: rash words spoken in the heat of debate
[…] Eusebius doth report that Ireneus dyd reprooue Victor byshop of Rome for his rash sentēce in excōmunicating the Churches of Grece, concerning the obseruation of the feast of Easter.

For ſitting in his [Marcus Junius Brutus's] tent, penſive and troubled vvith the horrour of his raſh act, it vvas not hard for him, ſlumbering in the cold, to dream of that vvhich moſt affrighted him; […]
[T]hrough the raſh adventure and fool-hardineſs of ſome fevv, an overture only made, and ſome advantage got of performing a great piece of ſervice and vvorthy exploit.
I vvas a fool, too raſh, and quite miſtaken / In vvhat I thought vvould have ſucceeded beſt.
He will tell you in how few moments ſhe repented of the raſh meſſage ſhe had ſent you— […]

So ſhould an ideot vvhile at large he ſtrays, / Find the ſvveet lyre on vvhich an artiſt plays, / VVith raſh and aukvvard force the chords he ſhakes, / And grins vvith vvonder at the jar he makes; […]

Take then no vow at random: ta'en, with faith / Preserve it; yet not bent, as Jephthah once, / Blindly to execute a rash resolve, / Whom better it had suited to exclaim, / 'I have done ill,' than to redeem his pledge / By doing worse: […]
She did a rash thing. She sent a letter to Ivy Bolton, enclosing a note to the keeper, and asking Mrs Bolton to give it to him.

glosses: Of corn or other grains: so dry as to fall out of the ear with handling.
Requiring swift action; pressing; urgent.

examples.text: My Lord, I ſcarce haue leiſure to ſalute you, / My matter is ſo raſh: […]

glosses: Taking effect quickly and strongly; fast-acting.

examples.text: [T]he vnited veſſel of their bloud, / […] / Shall neuer leake, though it doe vvorke as ſtrong, / As Aconitum, or raſh gunpovvder.

glosses: Synonym of rashly (“in a rash manner; hastily or without due consideration”).

examples.text: Soft Gooddie Sheepe (then ſaid the Foxe) not ſoe: / Vnto the King ſo raſh ye may not goe, / He is vvith greater matter buſied, / Than a Lambe, or the Lambes ovvne mothers hed.
VVhy do you ſpeake ſo ſtartingly and raſh?
But the right thing 'ud be for Tulliver to go and make it up with her himself, and say he was sorry for speaking so rash.

glosses: An area of inflamed and irritated skin characterized by reddened spots that may be filled with fluid or pus. Also, preceded by a descriptive word (rare or obsolete), an illness characterized by a type of rash.

examples.text: He came out in a rash because of an allergy.
She applied rash cream on herself to reduce the irritation.
A wet cloth should help with the rash on your arm.

glosses: An irregular distribution or sprinkling of objects resembling a rash (sense 1).
An outbreak or surge in problems; a spate, string, or trend.

examples.text: There has been a rash of vandalism lately.
Wet through and through: with her feet squelching and squashing in her shoes whenever she moved; with a rash of rain upon her classical visage; […]
Until the recent rash of North London line maps appeared on station billboards in the London area of BR, the service undoubtedly suffered from meagre and ineffectual publicity.

Science has tried and failed to come to a consensus about the hygienic superiority of one product over the other. Even so, the paper towel industry has funded or promoted a rash of studies claiming that hand dryers turn bathrooms into mosh pits of pathogens.
